name: Capstone design decisions
note: Three moments in a whiteboard 'design a production AI system' round. Pick the senior move before the chapter names it — each is a place candidates reveal their level.

items.prompt: Asked to design a production document-Q&A bot, a candidate opens with: 'I'd use a vector database, an embedding model, and a frontier LLM.'
candidates: Start with requirements and SLOs — scale (queries/day), latency target, cost ceiling, and a quality bar — because the architecture and every component choice follow from them; leading with boxes is the junior tell
That's a fine start; the components are what matter most
Ask which vector database the company already uses first
Begin by choosing the largest model to guarantee quality
items.correct: Start with requirements and SLOs — scale (queries/day), latency target, cost ceiling, and a quality bar — because the architecture and every component choice follow from them; leading with boxes is the junior tell
items.explanation: The strongest signal in a system-design round is leading with requirements and SLOs before architecture. 'p99 < 2s, under $X/month, groundedness ≥ 0.8 at 50K queries/day' makes every later choice defensible — model tier, cascade, self-host vs API — because each traces to a target. A candidate who opens with components is solving before they know what they're solving for.
items.principle: Requirements and SLOs first; the architecture is derived from them, not the other way around.

items.prompt: The proposed design routes every query to a single frontier model 'for the best quality.' The cost SLO is $500/month at 10K queries/day.
candidates: Frontier-everything blows the cost SLO (~$1,700/month here); route on a calibrated confidence — cheap model for the easy majority, escalate the hard queries — to hit the quality bar near the cost ceiling
Quality always wins; exceed the cost SLO and justify it later
Switch entirely to the cheap model to meet the cost SLO
Cache everything so the model choice doesn't matter
items.correct: Frontier-everything blows the cost SLO (~$1,700/month here); route on a calibrated confidence — cheap model for the easy majority, escalate the hard queries — to hit the quality bar near the cost ceiling
items.explanation: A design has to satisfy the cost SLO *and* the quality SLO together — defaulting to 'always frontier' ignores the first, and 'always cheap' ignores the second. The cascade (Chapter 4) is the lever that hits both: calibrated routing holds accuracy near frontier at a fraction of the bill. Naming the cascade — and the calibration it depends on — is the answer the cost ceiling demands.
items.principle: Defend each component against the SLOs it must satisfy; a cascade reconciles a quality bar with a cost ceiling.

items.prompt: The interviewer asks: 'What's the riskiest failure of this design, and how would you know it happened?'
candidates: Silent quality decay — the system stays up and fast while answers rot as the corpus ages — bounded by eval-in-prod (sampled, CI-gated) plus a drift monitor on rolling windows, because infra dashboards can't see it
The server going down, caught by an uptime monitor
Running out of GPU memory, caught by an OOM alert
There aren't really failure modes once it passes launch eval
items.correct: Silent quality decay — the system stays up and fast while answers rot as the corpus ages — bounded by eval-in-prod (sampled, CI-gated) plus a drift monitor on rolling windows, because infra dashboards can't see it
items.explanation: The riskiest failure of an AI system is the silent one: green dashboards, confidently wrong answers (Chapter 0). Naming it — and the specific mechanisms that catch it (sampled eval-in-prod, a rolling-window drift monitor on the quality signal) — demonstrates you know the AI-specific failure mode, not just the classical ones. 'It might go down' is true of any service; the silent quality failure is the one this guide exists for.
items.principle: The headline risk in an AI design is silent quality decay — name it, and the eval + drift machinery that makes it visible.
